stem: You are trying to loosen a nut using a spanner, but it is not working. In order to open the nut, you need to:

modelAnswer: A longer spanner gives a larger lever arm, so the same applied force produces a greater torque, making it easier to loosen or tighten large nuts. For a small nut, an extra-long wrench produces so much torque that it risks over-tightening or shearing the nut/bolt, so a shorter spanner giving a controlled torque is used instead.
stem: Why long spanner is used to open or tight nuts of vehicle's tyre? While tightening a small nut, extra-long wrench is not suitable. Why?

modelAnswer: Fixing the knob at the edge maximises the perpendicular distance from the hinge, so a small applied force produces enough torque to open the door easily. If the knob were at the middle, the lever arm would be halved, requiring much more force to produce the same turning effect.

keyPoints: Like parallel forces act in the same direction, e.g. two people pulling a rope the same way.
Unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions while remaining parallel, e.g. forces on the two ends of a seesaw.
Their resultants and turning effects (moments) differ: like forces add directly, unlike forces can produce a couple/turning effect.
modelAnswer: Like parallel forces act in the same direction, whereas unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions. Their resultant depends on their magnitudes and lines of action.
stem: Differentiate between like and unlike parallel forces.

keyPoints: Moment of force (torque) is the turning effect produced by a force about a pivot point.
It depends on the magnitude of the applied force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
Formula: Torque (tau) = Force (F) x perpendicular distance (d) from the pivot.
modelAnswer: Moment of force, or torque, is the turning effect of a force about a pivot. It depends on the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action: torque = force × perpendicular distance.
stem: What is moment of force or torque? On what factors it depends? Write its mathematical formula

modelAnswer: Torque = F x d = 50 N x 0.20 m = 10 N m. To produce the same 10 N m torque with 100 N: d = torque/F = 10/100 = 0.10 m = 10 cm. (Ans. 10 N m and 10 cm, as printed in the textbook.)
stem: Calculate the torque acting on spanner of length 20 cm to loosen a nut by a force of 50 N. If the same nut is to be loosened up by force of 100 N, what should be length of spanner?

modelAnswer: By the principle of moments: m1 x d1 = m2 x d2, so 0.6 kg x 0.2 m = m2 x 0.3 m, giving m2 = 0.12/0.3 = 0.4 kg. (Ans. 0.4 kg, as printed in the textbook.)
stem: A long uniform steel bar of length 1.0 m is balanced by a pivot at its middle. Two masses m1 and m2 are suspended at a distance of 0.2 m and 0.3 m respectively from the pivot. Ignoring mass of the steel bar, if mass m1 = 0.6 kg find mass m2.

The 400 g mass must be placed on the opposite side to balance this: distance = 6750/400 = 16.875 cm from the pivot, i.e. at the 50 - 16.9 = 33.1 cm mark. (Ans. 33.1 cm, as printed in the textbook.)

keyPoints: The center of mass is the point where the entire mass of a body can be considered to act, and about which mass is equally distributed.
Uniform mass distribution places the center of mass at the geometric center of a symmetric body.
Non-uniform mass distribution shifts the center of mass toward the region of greater mass concentration.
modelAnswer: The centre of mass is the point at which a body's mass may be considered concentrated. Changing the distribution of mass changes its position; it shifts toward the part containing more mass.
stem: Define center of mass. What is effect of mass distribution in a body on its center of mass?

keyPoints: Center of gravity is the point where the whole weight of a body appears to act.

For regular shapes: circular plate - center of the circle; rectangular/square plate - intersection of diagonals; triangular plate - centroid (intersection of medians); cylinder - midpoint of its axis; sphere - the geometric center.

Center of mass depends only on mass distribution, while center of gravity depends on the distribution of weight in a gravitational field; the two coincide when gravity is uniform across the body, as is the case for everyday objects near Earth's surface.
modelAnswer: The centre of gravity is the point through which the resultant weight acts. For a uniform circular, rectangular or square plate it is at the geometric centre; for a uniform triangle it is at the intersection of medians; for a uniform cylinder or sphere it is at its geometric centre. Centre of mass depends on mass distribution, while centre of gravity concerns the action of gravity and coincides with it in a uniform gravitational field.
stem: What is center of gravity? Where will be center of gravity of these regular shaped bodies; circular plate, rectangular and square shaped plate, triangular shaped plate, cylinder, sphere (also draw figures to support your answer). Differentiate between center of mass and center of gravity.

stem: A body in equilibrium must not have:

options.text: both in static and dynamic equilibrium

stem: A uniformly rotating fan is said to be in:

keyPoints: Equilibrium is the state of a body when the net force and net torque acting on it are both zero.

First condition of equilibrium: the vector sum of all forces acting on the body is zero (translational equilibrium). Second condition: the sum of all torques about any point is zero (rotational equilibrium).
The principle of moments states that for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same pivot.
modelAnswer: Equilibrium means that the net force and net torque on a body are zero. Thus translational equilibrium requires zero resultant force and rotational equilibrium requires zero resultant moment. The principle of moments states that, for equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.
stem: What is equilibrium? Describe the conditions of equilibrium. State an explain principle of moments.

explanation: A long horizontal pole lowers the center of gravity relative to the base and widens the effective base of support, maximising stability; the stem asks which configuration most affects (improves) stability.
stem: A tightrope walker is carrying a long pole while walking across a rope. The stability of the walker is affected if the pole is

modelAnswer: Legs spread apart provide better stability because they widen the base of support; a wider base keeps the vertical line through the center of gravity inside the base for a larger range of tilts, making you harder to push over.
stem: When standing on a crowded school bus, which stance would provide better stability and prevent you from being pushed over: legs joined or legs spread apart?

modelAnswer: A moving bicycle's spinning wheels have angular momentum, which resists changes in the orientation of the spin axis (gyroscopic effect), helping keep the bicycle upright. A stationary bicycle has no such angular momentum and topples easily.
stem: Why a moving bicycle is easier to balance? Relate this to the principles of rotational motion.

modelAnswer: A pencil on its tip has an extremely small base of support, so even a tiny displacement moves its center of gravity outside that base, producing a toppling moment. Stability of an object balanced on a point depends on the size of the base of support and the height of the center of gravity above it: a wider base and lower center of gravity give greater stability.
stem: Why is a pencil standing on its tip unstable, and what factors affect the stability of an object balanced on a point?

keyPoints: Stability improves by lowering the center of gravity and/or widening the base of support, so a larger tilt is needed before the center of gravity falls outside the base.
Examples: racing cars are built low and wide; a tightrope walker's pole widens the effective base and lowers the effective center of gravity; ships carry ballast low in the hull.
Everyday applications include furniture design, vehicle design and sports (e.g. a wrestler's wide stance).
modelAnswer: Stability is improved by lowering the centre of gravity and increasing the base area. Racing cars are low and wide, and a tightrope walker uses a long horizontal pole to improve stability. Buildings and vehicles use broad bases for the same reason.
stem: Propose how the stability of an object can be improved. Illustrate the applications of stability physics in real life.

explanation: A slippery surface has reduced friction, giving less grip and making walking (and stopping slipping) harder.
stem: It is more difficult to walk on a slippery surface than on a nonslippery one because of:

explanation: At terminal velocity, air resistance balances weight so the net force, and hence acceleration, is zero.
stem: For an object moving with terminal velocity, its acceleration:

explanation: Denser, heavier objects reach a higher terminal velocity before air resistance balances their weight; hailstones are densest/heaviest, snowflakes lightest, so Hailstone > Raindrop > Snowflake.
stem: The correct order of comparison for the terminal speeds of a raindrop, snowflake, and hailstone is:

modelAnswer: The feather reaches terminal velocity first because its low weight is quickly balanced by air resistance. The bowling ball, being much heavier, hits the ground first since it accelerates for longer before air resistance can significantly slow it.
stem: If you drop a feather and a bowling ball from the same height, which one will reach the terminal velocity first? Which one of them will hit the ground first?

modelAnswer: The narrow blade of an ice skate concentrates pressure and creates a thin slippery film that reduces friction with the ice, allowing smooth gliding. Shoes have a wider, rougher sole that grips normal ground surfaces (higher friction), which on ice instead causes skidding as friction is too low to control motion.
stem: Why do ice skates effortlessly slide on ice, while your shoes cause skidding?

modelAnswer: This is a printed textbook typo/reversal; physically it is easier to push a car with properly inflated tyres than flat ones. Flat tyres increase the contact area and deformation against the road, increasing rolling friction, so more force is needed to push the car; inflated tyres reduce this contact/deformation and hence the frictional resistance.
stem: Explain why it's easier to push a car on flat tyres than inflated ones. What happens to the frictional force between the tyres and the road?

keyPoints: Friction is the resistive force that opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact.

It is caused by microscopic irregularities and adhesive forces between contacting surfaces; advantages include walking, gripping, and braking, while disadvantages include energy loss as heat and wear of moving machine parts.
Friction can be reduced by lubrication, polishing surfaces, and using ball bearings/rollers to convert sliding friction into rolling friction.
modelAnswer: Friction is the force opposing relative motion between contacting surfaces. It is caused by surface irregularities and adhesion. It provides grip for walking and braking, but causes wear and energy loss. Lubricants, ball bearings and smoother surfaces reduce unwanted friction.
stem: Define force of friction. What causes friction? What are advantages and disadvantages of friction? Explain with examples. How can friction be reduced?

keyPoints: Sliding friction occurs when one surface slides over another (e.g. dragging a box); rolling friction occurs when a round object rolls over a surface (e.g. a ball or wheel).
Rolling friction is generally much smaller than sliding friction for the same surfaces and normal force, because rolling contact involves less relative surface displacement/deformation.
This is why ball bearings and wheels are used to reduce friction in machines and vehicles compared to dragging or sliding parts.
modelAnswer: Sliding friction occurs when surfaces slide over each other. Rolling friction occurs when an object rolls and is usually smaller because there is less surface rubbing. A box dragged on a floor has sliding friction, while a wheel on a road has rolling friction.
stem: Compare rolling friction and sliding friction. How are they different in terms of contact surfaces, motion, and forces involved? Explain with examples.

keyPoints: As an object falls, gravity accelerates it downward while air resistance (drag) increases with speed.
Initially net force and acceleration are large; as speed increases, drag grows until it equals the object's weight.
At that point net force is zero, acceleration becomes zero, and the object falls at a constant terminal velocity.
modelAnswer: As an object falls through a fluid, resistive force increases with speed. Eventually resistive force equals weight, so resultant force and acceleration become zero. The object then moves with constant terminal velocity.

modelAnswer: If a driver takes a curve too fast, the required centripetal force exceeds what friction between tyres and road can supply, and the car skids outward off its curved path. Friction supplies the centripetal force that keeps the car turning along the curve; as long as it is sufficient for the speed and radius, the car stays on the road.
stem: While driving what happens if the driver take the curve too fast? How does centripetal force play a role in keeping the car from skidding off the road?

modelAnswer: For a ball swung in a vertical circle, tension is greatest at the bottom (where tension must supply both the centripetal force and support against gravity) and smallest at the top (where gravity itself contributes toward the centripetal force). In a horizontal circle, tension supplies the centripetal force and stays roughly constant if speed is constant.
stem: Consider a situation where you swing a ball connected to a string in a circle. How does the tension in the string vary as the ball moves across different points in its circular path, and what forces are involved?

modelAnswer: A geostationary satellite must orbit at exactly the speed that matches Earth's rotation period at its orbital radius, so gravity provides exactly the centripetal force needed; only this specific speed keeps it above the same point on Earth continuously, which is essential for uninterrupted communication links.
stem: Why is it important for communication satellites in geostationary orbit to maintain a specific speed?

keyPoints: Centripetal force is the net force directed toward the center of a circular path, required to keep a body moving in that circle.
It continuously changes the direction of the body's velocity without changing its speed, producing centripetal (radial) acceleration.
Without this force the body would move off in a straight line tangent to the circle, by Newton's first law.
modelAnswer: Centripetal force is the inward resultant force that keeps an object moving in a circular path. It continually changes the direction of velocity toward the centre, producing centripetal acceleration.
stem: Define centripetal force. Describe the motion of a body in a circular path under the action of centripetal force.

keyPoints: For a car turning on a road, friction between tyres and road supplies the centripetal force.
For a satellite orbiting Earth, gravitational attraction supplies the centripetal force.
For a ball whirled on a string, tension in the string supplies the centripetal force; for electrons in an atom, electrostatic attraction plays this role.
modelAnswer: Examples of centripetal force include tension in a stone whirled on a string, friction between tyres and a road when a car turns, gravity keeping satellites in orbit, and electromagnetic attraction in charged-particle motion.
stem: Identify different sources of centripetal force in real life examples.

keyPoints: Orbital velocity is the speed a satellite needs to maintain a stable circular orbit at a given radius, where gravitational force exactly supplies the required centripetal force.
Scientists calculate the orbital speed for a target orbital radius (e.g. geostationary orbit) and launch/inject satellites at that speed and altitude so gravity keeps them in the intended path.
The chosen speed depends on the orbital radius (distance from Earth's center) and Earth's mass; higher orbits require lower orbital speeds.
modelAnswer: Orbital velocity is the speed required for an object to remain in orbit around a massive body. Scientists choose it so gravity supplies the required centripetal force. The required speed depends on the mass of the central body and the orbital radius; lower orbits require greater speed.
stem: Define orbital velocity. How do scientists use the concept of orbital speed to launch satellites into specific orbits? What factors influence the chosen speed?
